oneliner.t: Four-term Democratic congressman and former two-term Phoenix mayor (2012–2018), in the House since 2019; he beat progressive challenger Kai Newkirk 62.3%–37.7% in the July 21, 2026 primary and faces Republican Zuhdi Jasser and No Labels nominee Tisha Benoit in a district rated Solid/Safe D.

upbringing.t: Born on Long Island, New York; his family moved to Arizona and he graduated from Cortez High School in west Phoenix in 1988. He earned a history and political science degree from Marquette University (1992, magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa) and a law degree from the University of Michigan (1995), then worked as an education attorney before winning a Phoenix City Council seat in 2000. He is married to attorney Nicole Stanton; they have two children.

profile.office_years_note: Phoenix City Council 2000–2009, Arizona Deputy Attorney General 2009–2011 (appointed), Phoenix mayor Jan 2012–May 2018, U.S. House Jan 2019–present.

career.role: Mayor of Phoenix (resigned May 29, 2018 to run for Congress)
U.S. Representative, AZ-09 (2019–2023) and AZ-04 (2023–); Foreign Affairs; Transportation & Infrastructure

platform.t: Blames tariffs, Iran-war fuel costs and expired ACA tax credits for rising costs; proposes ending tariffs he calls an unauthorized tax, ending the Iran conflict legislatively, and restoring ACA credits.
Credits the Inflation Reduction Act's drug-price provisions; wants Medicare negotiation extended to all consumers and an end to AI-driven prior authorization in Medicare (the WISeR model).
Zoning reform, density near transit, faster permitting, down-payment aid, full funding of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit; cites bipartisan limits on corporate home buying.
Developers should pay all infrastructure, energy and environmental costs; opposes federal preemption of local zoning; supports ending federal tax breaks for data-center operators.

Voted against the July 2026 Massie amendment to cut military aid to Israel, saying it would undermine countering Iran, while criticizing Netanyahu and saying 'clear change is necessary' ahead of the 2028 MOU expiry.
Has a stated personal policy against owning individual stocks and backs a congressional stock-trading ban.

promises.t: Eliminate federal tariffs, end the Iran conflict through legislation and reinstate ACA premium tax credits.
Expand Medicare drug-price negotiation to all consumers; end AI algorithms in Medicare prior-authorization decisions.
Fully fund the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and add down-payment aid for first-time buyers.

city_races.t: Raised over $250,000 Jan 1–May 31, 2011, more than Neely (~$167K), Mattox (~$150K) and Gullett (~$116K) in that period. Wikipedia notes questions in the 2011 campaign about the legality of nearly $70,000 in contributions linked to a former campaign treasurer, Mindy Shields, whom he fired in Oct 2010 (details as summarized were unclear; not resolved here).

City filing for Stanton For Mayor (CAN-10-14), Jan 2015 report: $188,375.44 raised campaign-to-date; the two cash-on-hand fields on the form disagree ($338,821.68 vs $28,088.33). Final 2015 totals not located.

corp.t: PAC money every federal cycle: $411,907 (2018), $655,961 (2020), $1,250,681 (2022), $806,686 (2024), $638,725 (2025–Jul 1, 2026), about 27% of career receipts. The Prospect reports over $600,000 from corporate PACs this cycle (UnitedHealth, Amazon, Google, Walmart, Boeing, RTX); Legis1 lists utility (Pinnacle West, SRP), Honeywell and apartment-industry PACs alongside union PACs. An AI-industry super PAC network (Leading the Future, funded by Greg Brockman, Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz and others) spent about $227,000 for him in the primary ($592,221 per the Transformer tracker). No reporting links this money to a specific vote.

lobby.t: Track AIPAC lists $321,822 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, DMFI, GCSC, JAC, J Street, PIA) and their large donors; $0 in independent expenditures. The Prospect reports $6,000 directly from AIPAC's PAC this cycle.
